title: Predicted reverse-mex behavior for three families of subtraction Nim with a pass
statement: Consider subtraction Nim with subtraction set $\{s_1,s_2,s_3\}$ and one pass. Let $\mathcal{G}(x,0)$ denote the Grundy number without a pass and $\mathcal{G}(x,1)$ the Grundy number with a pass. The source defines the relevant reverse-$mex$ recurrences by equations $(1)$–$(3)$. **The three-family prediction.** (a) For subtraction set $\{s_1,s_2,s_3\}=\{a,2an,2an+a\}$ with $a,n\in\mathbb{N}$, equation $(1)$ holds, and for $x\geq6an+(4a+1)$ equations $(2)$ and $(3)$ hold; the Grundy sequence enters a loop at that threshold. (b) For subtraction set $\{a,(2n+1)a,(2n+3)a\}$ with $a,n\in\mathbb{N}$, equation $(1)$ holds, and for $x\geq a(2n+3)+1$ equations $(2)$ and $(3)$ hold; moreover $\mathcal{G}(x,1)<4$ for every $x$, and the sequence enters a loop at that threshold. (iii) For subtraction set $\{a,(2n+1)a,(2n+5)a\}$ with $a,n\in\mathbb{N}$, equation $(1)$ holds, $\mathcal{G}(x,1)<4$ for every $x$, and for $x\geq a(2n+5)+1$ equations $(2)$ and $(3)$ hold; the sequence enters a loop at that threshold. These are examples and predictions based on computer calculations; the source does not establish them as theorems or report a resolution.

source_name: Urban Larsson, Hikaru Manabe and Ryohei Miyadera, “A Subtraction Nim with a Pass”, arXiv:2605.14321 (2026).

progress.label: Open · solution reported
progress.tldr: An unverified posted calculation claims all three predictions fail, while the only published work proves a different special case.
progress.summary:
Larsson, Manabe, and Miyadera (2026) state the three families as Conjecture 3, based on examples and computer calculations rather than proofs. The conjecture predicts reverse-$\mathrm{mex}$ recurrences, bounds, and eventual looping for the specified subtraction sets.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14321)*

**Known results**

- Larsson, Manabe, and Miyadera (2026) prove the separate case $\{2,4n,4n+2\}$ for $n\geq3$, including the one-pass game and eventual periodic behavior from $x\geq12n+9$; this does not establish Conjecture 3.

*[arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.14321v1) · [doi.org](https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.14321)*

**Posted attempt**

An unverified calculation claims explicit counterexamples within the stated ranges: $(a,n)=(1,2)$ for family (a), $(1,1)$ for family (b), and $(1,2)$ for family (iii), with scaling extending them to every positive $a$. If correct, this disproves all three universal predictions; it has not been independently verified.

Current status (as of August 2026): The three-family assertions remain unproved, and an unverified calculation claims counterexamples to all three; no verified resolution is recorded.

*Caveats. The counterexamples appear only in reader-written material, not in a verified mathematical publication.*

solutions.body:
**All three stated families have infinitely many counterexamples.**

For a subtraction set \(S\), let \(g_S(x)\) and \(h_S(x)\) be the Grundy values without and with one available pass. The source's recurrences are

\[
g_S(0)=h_S(0)=0,
\]

\[
g_S(x)=\operatorname{mex}\{g_S(x-s):s\in S,\ s\le x\},
\]

and, for \(x>0\),

\[
h_S(x)
=\operatorname{mex}
\left(
\{h_S(x-s):s\in S,\ s\le x\}
\cup\{g_S(x)\}
\right).
\tag{1}
\]

All three conjectured families claim that after their respective thresholds the pass option can be omitted:

\[
h_S(x)
=\operatorname{mex}\{h_S(x-s):s\in S\}.
\tag{2}
\]

Each assertion fails inside its explicitly claimed range.

**Family (a).** Choose \(n=2\), \(a=1\), so \(S=\{1,4,5\}\) and the threshold is \(6an+4a+1=17\). Exact mex recursion gives

\[
h_S(18)=4,
\qquad
\operatorname{mex}\{h_S(17),h_S(14),h_S(13)\}
=\operatorname{mex}\{2,3,1\}=0.
\]

**Family (b).** Choose \(n=1\), \(a=1\), so \(S=\{1,3,5\}\) and the threshold is \(a(2n+3)+1=6\). Then

\[
h_S(6)=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{mex}\{h_S(5),h_S(3),h_S(1)\}
=\operatorname{mex}\{2,2,2\}=0.
\]

**Family (iii).** Choose \(n=2\), \(a=1\), so \(S=\{1,5,9\}\) and the threshold is \(a(2n+5)+1=10\). Then

\[
h_S(10)=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{mex}\{h_S(9),h_S(5),h_S(1)\}
=\operatorname{mex}\{2,2,2\}=0.
\]

Moreover, direct induction in (1) proves, for every positive integer \(a\),

\[
g_{aS}(aj)=g_S(j),
\qquad
h_{aS}(aj)=h_S(j).
\]

Therefore these counterexamples extend to all positive \(a\):

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c}
\text{family}&n&S&x&\text{threshold}\\ \hline
(a)&2&\{a,4a,5a\}&18a&16a+1\\
(b)&1&\{a,3a,5a\}&6a&5a+1\\
(iii)&2&\{a,5a,9a\}&10a&9a+1 .
\end{array}
\]

In every row \(x\) meets its claimed threshold and (2) fails. Conjecture 3 explicitly quantifies \(a,n\in\mathbb N\); the earlier restriction \(n\ge3\) belongs to a different proved special case. These counterexamples concern the explicitly included small-\(n\) cases; they do not assert failure after adding the extra restriction \(n\ge3\).

Source: Larsson, Manabe, and Miyadera, *A Subtraction Nim with a Pass*, equations (35)–(37) and Conjecture 3, https://arxiv.org/html/2605.14321 .
